free.title: DOMINO PARK
free.caption:
FREE · DOMINO PARK

Williamsburg's free waterfront park is built right on top of an old sugar empire, and most people walking through have no idea.

Domino Park sits on the site of the Domino Sugar Refinery, once the largest sugar refinery in the world, refining up to 4 million pounds of sugar a day before it closed in 2004. The team behind the High Line spent six years turning it into 6 free acres: an elevated walkway resting on real salvaged warehouse columns, syrup tanks kept as sculpture, a dog run, bocce, beach volleyball, and a wide lawn facing the Manhattan skyline across the East River.

Go right before sunset - the light hits the old refinery brick and the water at the same time.

Save this for your next free Sunday, it beats paying for a rooftop view.

📷 Domino Park

food.title: NOM WAH TEA PARLOR
food.caption:
FOOD · NOM WAH TEA PARLOR

Chinatown's first dim sum parlor has been on the same corner of Doyers St since 1920, and the paper order menu still hasn't changed the way you fill it out.

Nom Wah opened as a tea and dim sum counter in 1920, moved to its current spot around the corner in the 1960s, and is now run by the fourth generation of the same family. The dim sum menu runs all day, not just brunch hours - roast pork buns, hand-folded Shanghainese soup dumplings, and har gow all under $5 a plate, checked off on a paper menu at your table.

Go on a weekday afternoon and you can usually walk right in, no line down Doyers St.

Save this before your next Chinatown wander - it's the one dim sum spot every local already has memorized.

📷 Nom Wah Tea Parlor

art.title: 6 SECRETS OF TRINITY CHURCH
art.caption:
HIDDEN GEM · TRINITY CHURCH

The church at the head of Wall Street ruled the Manhattan skyline for 44 years, and most people rushing past on their lunch break have never looked up.

Trinity Church is free to walk into, and its churchyard holds Alexander Hamilton's grave steps from the trading floor. This Gothic Revival building - the third on the same site - went up in 1846 and stayed NYC's tallest structure until 1890. Its bronze doors were cast by three different sculptors, and a stone cherub on the Church St gate was salvaged from a London church bombed in the Blitz.

Three blocks north, its own St. Paul's Chapel has stood since 1766 - older than Trinity's own building.

Save this before your next Financial District walk - the spire you pass every day has more history than half the museums downtown.

📷 Trinity Church Wall Street
